title: Amid Shortage of Counselors, Students Need Stronger Networks, Not More Chatbots ks-not-more-chatbots/
author: Julia Freeland Fisher
summary: Freeland Fisher starts from a ratio that will not fix itself: national student-to-counselor numbers improved one percent last year, which puts the recommended 250 to 1 target more than thirty years away. Schools and students have already responded by turning to chatbots, and her argument is that this substitution preserves the wrong design. The real flaw is the one-to-many advising model itself, and AI's better use is to build a many-to-one model in which teachers, alumni, family, mentors and employers all surround a single student. She reports findings from a pilot with ten college and career guidance platforms, which produced three lessons. Students first need help seeing the network they already have, and the mapping data is revealing: family and teachers accounted for forty percent of selections while counselors made up ten percent and peers four. Second, outreach has to feel authentic, and more than half of students wanted to thank a supporter before asking for anything. Third, students need coaching and warm introductions to convert a contact into support. Her policy point is that no state request for proposals currently names stronger student networks as a desired outcome, which is what actually determines what vendors build.
points: Reframes the counselor shortage as a design problem rather than a staffing problem, arguing chatbots simply automate a one-to-many model that never worked.
Reports network-mapping data showing family and teachers dominate the relationships students can name while counselors account for about ten percent and work or alumni connections almost none.
Finds that authenticity governs whether students engage a network, with 53 percent wanting to express gratitude first and only 14 percent making an outright request for help.
Distinguishes chatbots that give postsecondary advice from ones built to rehearse a real conversation and raise the confidence to contact a person.
Identifies procurement as the lever, since no state request for proposals yet asks advising technology to grow and measure students' human networks.
quotes: In the last school year, the national student-to-school counselor ratio improved by a meager 1% — from 376 to 372 students per counselor.

Turning to tech is rational when human resources are scarce. But swapping chatbots for overworked counselors masks a more fundamental problem: For decades, schools have tried to make a one-to-many advising model work.

AI could be a tool to help schools create something different: a many-to-one model in which each young person is surrounded by a strong network of teachers, alumni, family, mentors, employers, coaches and counselors working together to help students make progress.
Family and teacher connections together accounted for 40% of selections; counselors made up just 10%, peers only 4%.

Second, connection has to feel authentic. Even after students identify who’s in their corner (and who they might be missing), it’s often hard to get them to engage with those connections. The thing that mattered most: authenticity. Students didn’t want outreach to feel transactional or one-sided.

For example, ESAI ‘s team discovered that after identifying “people in their corner,” over half (53%) of students first wanted to express gratitude to those supporters before asking them for something. Only 14% made an outright request for help.

To date, no state-level request for proposals — the documents that steer what ed tech companies actually build — lists stronger student networks as a desired outcome for college and career advising tools.
We could wait 30 years for the counselor ratio to reach 250:1. Or we could start building toward a different ratio altogether: many people, supporting every one student.
